title: Og Falls, the Land Is Divided, and Moses Is Refused
summary: Moses recalls the defeat of Og, king of Bashan, and the capture of his sixty fortified cities, then describes how the conquered land east of the Jordan was given to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh on condition that their fighting men cross over with the rest of Israel. He tells Joshua not to fear, pleads with God to let him enter the land himself, and is told to climb Pisgah, look, and commission Joshua instead.
story: Deuteronomy opens with Moses looking back over the forty years since Horeb (Deuteronomy's name for Mount Sinai). Chapter 2 told how Israel passed Edom, Moab, and Ammon peacefully and then defeated Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon. Chapter 3 finishes that review with the second victory, over Og, and it turns those two battles into a pledge: the God who gave Israel the land east of the Jordan will give them the land west of it. The chapter also closes a door. Moses, who has led the people since Egypt, asks one last time to cross the river and is refused. From here on the book is his farewell, and the story's weight shifts toward Joshua, who will lead the people over the Jordan in the book that bears his name.
historical:
The events recalled here are told more briefly in Numbers 21:33-35 and Numbers 32. Bashan was the high, well-watered plateau east of the Sea of Galilee and north of the Yarmuk River, in what is now southern Syria and the Golan Heights. Elsewhere the Bible remembers it for its cattle and its oaks (Amos 4:1; Isaiah 2:13). Edrei, where Og met Israel, is usually identified with modern Daraa in southern Syria. The region of Argob, with its sixty walled towns, lay somewhere in Bashan; its exact extent is uncertain. Gilead is the hill country south of Bashan, divided by the Jabbok River, and the Arnon Valley, the deep gorge that runs into the Dead Sea from the east, marked the southern edge of Israel's holdings. Rabbah of the Ammonites, where Og's great bed was said to be kept, is the site of modern Amman, the capital of Jordan.

Several asides in the chapter explain names and remember landmarks "to this day" (verse 14), and verse 11 speaks of Og's bed as something a reader could still go and see. Those who hold that Moses wrote the book usually take these as notes added by a later editor; those who see the book as shaped in the seventh century BC or later take them as signs of the book's own vantage point. Either way, the notes show a text written for readers who knew the geography and wanted it tied to the past.
cultural:
Og is called the last of the Rephaim (verse 11). In the Bible the Rephaim are a people of the land's distant past, remembered as tall and formidable (compare Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 20-21). The same word is also used for the shades of the dead (for example Isaiah 14:9), and texts from the ancient city of Ugarit on the Syrian coast use a related term for deceased heroes or royal ancestors. For an Israelite reader, then, Og was a figure out of legend, and his defeat said something about the God who beat him. His bed of iron measured nine cubits by four, roughly thirteen feet by six (a cubit was the length of a forearm, about eighteen inches). Some interpreters take it as a literal bed, a showpiece of a king's size and wealth, since iron was precious in the Late Bronze Age. Others suggest a funerary couch or sarcophagus, possibly of the dark basalt common in that region, which could be described as iron-like. The text doesn't settle it.

Verse 6 uses the language of the ban, cherem, in which a conquered city and its people were devoted to God and destroyed rather than taken as plunder or slaves. Israel was not alone in this practice. The Mesha Stele, an inscription set up by a Moabite king in the ninth century BC, boasts that Mesha devoted the population of an Israelite town to his god Chemosh. Here the ban covers the people but not the livestock and goods, which Israel keeps (verse 7). The grant of land to Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh also reflects tribal custom: land was held by clans and passed down within them, which is why Jair can name a cluster of villages after himself (Havvoth-jair means the tent villages of Jair).
literary: The chapter is first-person memoir, Moses speaking to the people in front of him, and it is built from a series of scenes each opened by the phrase "at that time" (verses 4, 8, 12, 18, 21, 23). The first half is battle report and land survey, dense with names. The second half narrows from the tribes, to Joshua, to Moses alone at prayer. Two words repeat through the whole: cross over, and see. The eastern tribes' soldiers must cross; Joshua has seen what God did; Moses asks to cross and see, and is allowed only to see. The parenthetical notes (verses 9, 11, 13-14) slow the account like a narrator leaning in to explain a map.

outline.t: The defeat of Og, king of Bashan
The land taken east of the Jordan, and Og's bed
The land given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh
The eastern tribes must fight for their brothers
Moses pleads to enter and is refused

doctrines.note: The victory over Og is credited to God before it is credited to Israel: "I have delivered him into your hand" (verse 2). Past deliverance becomes the ground for present courage, as Moses tells Joshua that the LORD "Himself will fight for you" (verse 22).

Moses prays with praise first, confessing that no god in heaven or on earth acts like the LORD, and only then asks. God refuses him, yet the refusal is not silence: God gives him the view from Pisgah and a task for Joshua. The chapter shows an honest prayer answered with no, and a faithful servant who accepts it.

Moses says God was angry with him on account of the people (verse 26), which recalls his failure at Meribah told in Numbers 20. Even the greatest leader in Israel's story stands under the same holy God as everyone else, and his office does not exempt him.

words.note: Charam, to devote to destruction. The verb means to set something apart for God so completely that it is removed from ordinary use, in war usually by destroying it. The related noun is cherem. It is one of the hardest words in the Old Testament, and it appears here for a whole population (verse 6). See the hard question below.

Rephaim, the name of an ancient people remembered as giants, and elsewhere a word for the dead. Calling Og the last of the Rephaim casts him as the survivor of a frightening past. The earlier generation had refused to enter the land for fear of such people (Deuteronomy 1:28); this generation watched God defeat one.

Nuach, to rest or settle. Moses promises that the eastern tribes may go home once God gives rest to their brothers (verse 20). Rest in Deuteronomy means secure life in the land, free from enemies, and it becomes one of the Bible's great words of hope, taken up in Psalm 95 and Hebrews 3 to 4.

Chazaq, to strengthen or make firm. God tells Moses to encourage and strengthen Joshua (verse 28). The same verb becomes the refrain of Joshua's commissioning in Deuteronomy 31 and Joshua 1: be strong and courageous. Leadership passes not only by appointment but by one man putting courage into another.

christ: Joshua's name, Yehoshua, means the LORD saves, and in Greek it is the same name as Jesus. The Letter to the Hebrews plays on this, noting that Joshua gave Israel rest in the land and yet the rest God promised was still to come (Hebrews 4:8-9), which it finds in Christ. The pattern of the chapter also points forward thematically: Moses, the giver of the law, can see the promised land but cannot bring the people into it; another leader must take them across. Christians have read this as a picture of the law's limits and of the need for a greater Joshua, though the chapter itself makes no prediction. Many readers have also noticed that Moses, refused entry here, appears in the land at last on the mountain of the transfiguration, talking with Jesus (Matthew 17:3).

hard.q: How can God command the killing of men, women, and children in the conquest of Og's cities?
hard.a:
The chapter says plainly that Israel struck down every inhabitant of Og's towns (verse 6), and a modern reader rightly recoils. Several responses are offered by those who take the text seriously. Some stress that the conquest is presented as a unique act of divine judgment on nations whose wickedness God had long tolerated (Genesis 15:16 speaks of the iniquity of the Amorites not yet being complete), not a pattern for later wars; Deuteronomy 20 limits it to the land itself. Some argue that the language of total destruction is conventional war rhetoric in the ancient Near East, as inscriptions like the Mesha Stele show, and note that Joshua and Judges report Canaanites still living in the land long after, which suggests hyperbole rather than literal extermination. Others hold that the texts reflect God accommodating himself to Israel's world while moving his people toward the fuller revelation of love for enemies in Christ.

None of these answers removes the difficulty entirely, and readers differ over which carries most weight. What Christians agree on is that no one may appeal to these chapters to justify violence today: the New Testament gives the church no land to conquer and no enemy to destroy, and it calls believers to overcome evil with good.

questions: Moses tells Joshua that what his own eyes have seen God do should shape how he faces what lies ahead. What past experiences of God's faithfulness do you need to remember before facing something new?
The eastern tribes already had their land but were asked to fight until their brothers had theirs too. What would it look like to stay committed to others after your own needs are met?
God refused Moses' request but let him see the land and prepare his successor. How do you respond when a heartfelt prayer is answered with no?
